tensions.title: Ship a UI fix for the toleration trap now, or hold for a mechanism-level Layer 4 fix
tensions.description: voting-requirements.md R2.6 names toleration/abstention/silence as arithmetically identical at Layer 3, Layer 4 and re-ratification. The dashboard and forms can be made to say this more clearly (already partly done: .yesonly styling). But R2.6 itself says plainly it 'cannot be fixed by form help text alone' because the same four words mean different things under different procedures. A structural fix (changing what toleration counts as, or splitting the position set by procedure) requires a Layer 4 amendment, which needs two endorsing reviews and 7 days -- a window that competes directly with the only remaining amendment slot before the 23 November re-ratification deadline.

pole_a.position: Ship the UI/copy fix immediately. It is the only lever available before 2 November regardless of what else the Lab decides, it costs nothing structurally, and every member who reads the dashboard between now and any mechanism fix is better off for having read a sharper warning than a duller one.
arguments: Ability cost of a copy/styling fix is near zero and ships today; a Layer 4 fix costs a 7-day window the Lab may not have free
B=MAP: even a perfect eventual mechanism fix does nothing for anyone voting between now and then
Doing the cheap thing now does not foreclose doing the structural thing later

pole_b.position: A confident, well-styled UI warning risks making the Lab feel R2.6 is closed when the structural fact -- toleration/abstention/silence are the same number where it matters most -- is untouched. If that false sense of closure means the Layer 4 fix never gets proposed before the calendar runs out, the UI fix made things worse, not better, because it spent the Lab's remaining trust in the page on a problem that still exists underneath it.
arguments: R2.6's own text: 'it cannot be fixed by form help text alone' -- the requirements doc already anticipated this exact move and rejected it as sufficient

A toleration genuinely does different work at Tier C (helps reach quorum without diluting majority) than at Layer 3/4/re-ratification (counts as nothing) -- no static copy on a dropdown or a dashboard row can be procedure-aware everywhere a member encounters the word
The Lab's attention and trust in the dashboard are finite resources; spending them on a fix that looks complete but isn't is a real cost, not a neutral one

tensions.conditions_favoring_a: If no Layer 4 window can realistically be found before 23 November regardless of this decision, shipping the cheap fix dominates -- something is strictly better than nothing when the alternative is certainly not happening.
tensions.conditions_favoring_b: If the Lab is going to bundle any structural fix into the re-ratification package anyway (same vote, same 10-of-14 threshold), shipping a confident UI fix first risks the Lab deciding the bundled structural item is no longer necessary -- precisely the false-closure risk pole B names.

tensions.title: Is dashboard polish the right use of the Lab's remaining attention at all
tensions.description: voting-requirements.md's own critical-path analysis ranks the Section 3.2 election as the only thing that matters by 2 November and explicitly calls dashboard/UX work 'off the critical path' (critical path item 3, after the election and identity columns). This panel itself produced five dashboard/UX recommendations. The tension is whether producing them -- and acting on them -- is a reasonable use of a small amount of cheap attention, or exactly the kind of legible, demoable, satisfying work that crowds out the illegible, un-automatable, calendar-bound task the deadline actually depends on: getting fourteen people to actually rank-vote in an election that is 'not code' at all.

pole_a.position: The five findings are cheap enough (CSS, one JS function, prose edits -- no new infrastructure, no server, nothing that needs maintaining after the cohort disperses) that they do not meaningfully compete with the time needed to chase the election. Fixing them is close to free and the UI does matter for the ordinary Tier C and Layer 3 business the Lab will keep doing regardless of the election's outcome.
arguments: None of the five findings require new infrastructure; all are bounded, same-day changes
The dashboard will still be read for every ordinary vote after 2 November whatever happens to the interim offices, so the fixes have value independent of the election timeline
Not every hour spent on this is an hour not spent on the election -- different people, different skills, can work on both in parallel

pole_b.position: This very panel is an instance of the problem it should be naming: a polished, line-numbered, well-argued review of a dashboard is exactly the kind of legible, reviewable, satisfying artifact that attracts attention, while 'post once to the governance channel and get fourteen busy people to actually rank three candidates on OpaVote' has no equivalent artifact, no line number, nothing to point at -- so it is systematically under-attended relative to its actual importance.
arguments: voting-requirements.md's own critical path explicitly ranks this work below the election and says so in terms

Fogg's own model: the election has high ability (nothing technical required) but low, diffuse motivation and no prompt firing at the right moment -- exactly the profile of a task that gets crowded out by more legible work, not a coincidence

There is no artifact for 'did the Convener post the candidate call-for-interest to the channel today' the way there is an artifact (a PR, a diff, a line number) for a dashboard fix -- illegible work is structurally under-rewarded by exactly the kind of review this panel is

tensions.conditions_favoring_a: If the Lab has distinct people available for dashboard work versus election-chasing (i.e. attention is not actually a single shared pool), the tension dissolves and both should proceed.
tensions.conditions_favoring_b: If the same one or two technically-minded members who would fix the dashboard are also the ones who would otherwise be posting reminders and chasing candidates, the tension is real and the election should win every time.

tensions.title: Should the dashboard disclose which positions were Convener-transcribed
tensions.description: Two members lack push access and must have their positions recorded by the Convener, per Constitution Section 1's 'reasonably equivalent route.' This is currently visible only in git commit history (votes/pr-{n}.md's log), never on the rendered dashboard -- voteOf() in docs/index.html parses only the position string in the table, never who committed it. Whether to surface this on the page a Record Keeper and every other member actually looks at is a genuinely two-sided question with no clean win.

pole_a.position: Disclose it. Ostrom's monitoring design principle holds that the people a rule protects should be able to see it working, not just trust that it is; a Record Keeper verifying under Section 3 should not have to go spelunking in git log to find evidence quality is uneven across rows.
arguments: The information already exists and is already public (commit history); surfacing it on the dashboard changes visibility, not privacy
A Record Keeper's verification job is explicitly to check the process happened correctly -- disclosure makes that checkable without extra effort
The current state (disclosed in git, invisible on the dashboard) was not chosen on purpose by anyone -- it is an accident of what voteOf() happens to parse, not a decision

pole_b.position: Don't. It permanently and publicly marks the two specific members who need the Section 1 fallback, in a world-readable repository, as the ones who needed help -- in a fourteen-person house where everyone will know who they are within a day regardless, making the disclosure a label with no protective value and a real stigma cost.
arguments: Section 1's entire point in providing a 'reasonably equivalent route' is that using it should not cost the member anything -- a visible label is a cost

Fixing the two members' actual access (R4.4-R4.5's real recommendation) resolves the underlying problem; disclosing the workaround instead of fixing the access gap treats a symptom as though it were acceptable to live with
Even B.J. Fogg -- whose seat's reflex is normally more transparency, less friction -- did not endorse disclosure once the stigma cost was named

tensions.conditions_favoring_a: If the two members themselves want it visible (e.g. to make clear their position was faithfully transcribed, not altered), disclosure serves them rather than exposing them -- this depends on consent this panel cannot obtain.
tensions.conditions_favoring_b: If access can be fixed quickly (granting the two members push rights is a far smaller task than any code change here), the right move is to close the gap rather than decide whether to disclose a workaround that should become unnecessary within days.
